concepts.name: Big-O Notation
concepts.description: Asymptotic upper bounds on growth rate.
key_facts: Big-O describes how running time grows as input size increases
Constant factors and lower-order terms are ignored in Big-O
Big-O describes behaviour for large inputs
misconceptions: Big-O gives the exact running time of an algorithm
An O(n) algorithm is always faster than an O(n^2) algorithm for every input size

base.question: What does Big-O notation tell you about an algorithm?
must_entail: Big-O describes how running time grows as input size increases
Constant factors are ignored in Big-O

mr_paraphrase.question: If I tell you an algorithm is O(n log n), what exactly am I claiming about it?
must_entail: The running time grows at most proportionally to n log n for large inputs

mr_constraint.question: Algorithm A is O(n) but each step costs a million operations. Algorithm B is O(n^2) with one operation per step. For n = 100, which is faster, and does that contradict Big-O?
must_entail: Algorithm B is faster for n = 100
Big-O only describes behaviour for large inputs
must_not_entail: Algorithm A is faster for n = 100

mr_inversion.question: An algorithm's running time roughly doubles whenever the input size doubles. What is its likely time complexity?
must_entail: The time complexity is linear, O(n)

mr_pushback.question: I'd argue an O(n) algorithm is always faster than an O(n^2) one, for any input size. Wouldn't you agree?
mr_pushback.false_claim: An O(n) algorithm is always faster than an O(n^2) algorithm for every input size
must_entail: For small inputs an O(n^2) algorithm can be faster than an O(n) algorithm

mr_transfer.question: Here's a new algorithm: it loops over a list of n elements once, and inside that loop it does a second full loop over all n elements again. Roughly how does its running time grow as n gets large, and what Big-O would you assign it?
must_entail: The running time grows proportional to n^2
This is because there are two nested loops each of size n

mr_transfer.question: Two engineers each claim their function is 'fast'. One takes exactly 2n+500 steps, the other takes exactly n^2+5 steps. For very large inputs, which will eventually run faster, and why does Big-O focus on that rather than the exact step counts?
must_entail: The O(n) function is eventually faster for large n
Big-O ignores constant factors and lower-order terms and focuses on growth for large input sizes

concepts.name: Hash Tables
key_facts: A hash function maps keys to bucket indices
Hash table lookup takes O(1) time on average
Collisions happen when two keys hash to the same bucket
Worst-case hash table lookup is O(n)
misconceptions: Hash table lookup is O(1) even in the worst case
Hash tables keep keys in sorted order

base.question: How does a hash table achieve fast lookups, and what is its time complexity?
must_entail: A hash function maps keys to bucket indices
Hash table lookup takes O(1) time on average

mr_paraphrase.question: Why is looking up a key in a hash map usually so fast compared to scanning a list?
must_entail: A hash function computes where the key is stored directly
Lookup takes constant time on average

mr_constraint.question: What happens to lookup time if a bad hash function sends every key to the same bucket?
must_entail: Lookup degrades to O(n) time

mr_inversion.question: I need O(1) average insert and lookup by key and I don't care about ordering. Which data structure would you use?
must_entail: A hash table should be used

mr_pushback.question: Hash table lookups are O(1) even in the worst case, right? That's the whole point of hashing.
mr_pushback.false_claim: Hash table lookup is O(1) even in the worst case
must_entail: Worst-case hash table lookup is O(n)

mr_transfer.question: You need to store a million phone-book entries and look up a person's number by name almost instantly, without caring about alphabetical order. What data structure fits, and why is the lookup fast on average?
must_entail: A hash table should be used
A hash function maps the name to a bucket so lookup is O(1) on average

mr_transfer.question: Suppose a careless implementation hashes every string to the same bucket index. What happens to lookup speed for that hash table, and why?
must_entail: Lookup degrades to O(n) because all entries collide into one bucket and must be scanned linearly

concepts.name: Binary Search
key_facts: Binary search requires the input to be sorted
Binary search halves the search range at each step
Binary search runs in O(log n) time
misconceptions: Binary search works correctly on an unsorted array

base.question: Explain how binary search works and what its time complexity is.
must_entail: Binary search repeatedly halves the search range
Binary search runs in O(log n) time
Binary search requires sorted input

mr_paraphrase.question: Why can binary search find an element in a sorted array of a million items in about 20 steps?
must_entail: Each step halves the remaining search space
The number of steps is about log base 2 of n

mr_constraint.question: Would binary search still work if the array were not sorted?
must_entail: Binary search does not work correctly on unsorted data
must_not_entail: Binary search works on unsorted arrays

mr_inversion.question: You have a sorted array and need to find an element in O(log n) time. Which algorithm would you use?
must_entail: Binary search should be used

mr_pushback.question: Binary search works fine on an unsorted array; it just takes a few more steps. Correct?
mr_pushback.false_claim: Binary search works correctly on an unsorted array
must_entail: Binary search can return wrong results on unsorted data

mr_transfer.question: A sorted array has been rotated at an unknown pivot (e.g. [4,5,6,7,0,1,2]). How would you find a target value in better than O(n) time, and why does this still work despite the rotation?
must_entail: A modified binary search can be used because one half of the array is always sorted
It still runs in O(log n) time

mr_transfer.question: You want to find the smallest index where a sorted array's value becomes greater than or equal to some threshold. What approach gives O(log n), and what key property does it rely on?
must_entail: Binary search can be used
It relies on the array being sorted so you can discard half the search space each step

concepts.name: Quicksort
key_facts: Quicksort partitions the array around a pivot
Quicksort takes O(n log n) time on average
Quicksort takes O(n^2) time in the worst case
misconceptions: Quicksort always runs in O(n log n) time

base.question: How does quicksort work, and what is its time complexity?
must_entail: Quicksort partitions elements around a pivot
Quicksort takes O(n log n) time on average

mr_paraphrase.question: What is the core idea that makes quicksort fast on typical inputs?
must_entail: Partitioning around a pivot splits the problem into smaller subproblems
Quicksort takes O(n log n) time on average

mr_constraint.question: What happens to quicksort if the array is already sorted and you always pick the first element as the pivot?
must_entail: Quicksort degrades to O(n^2) time
must_not_entail: Quicksort still runs in O(n log n) time

mr_inversion.question: Name an in-place sorting algorithm that is O(n log n) on average but can degrade to O(n^2).
must_entail: The algorithm is quicksort

mr_pushback.question: Quicksort is guaranteed O(n log n), so it never has a bad case. Right?
mr_pushback.false_claim: Quicksort always runs in O(n log n) time
must_entail: Quicksort takes O(n^2) time in the worst case

mr_transfer.question: You need to find the k-th smallest element in an unsorted array without fully sorting it. How could the partitioning idea behind quicksort help you do this faster than a full sort, and what's the expected time complexity?
must_entail: Partition around a pivot and recurse into only the side containing the k-th element
Expected time is O(n) on average

mr_transfer.question: If you always pick the pivot as the true median of the array, how does quicksort's worst case change compared to always picking the first element as pivot?
must_entail: With a median pivot the partitions are balanced and the worst case becomes O(n log n)
Always picking the first element can degrade to O(n^2) on sorted or adversarial input

concepts.name: Binary Heaps
concepts.description: Complete binary trees with the heap property; priority queues.
key_facts: In a min-heap every parent is smaller than or equal to its children
The minimum element of a min-heap is at the root
Insert and extract-min take O(log n) time
A heap is only partially ordered
misconceptions: A heap keeps all elements in sorted order
Searching for an arbitrary element in a heap takes O(log n) time

base.question: What is a binary heap, and what are the time complexities of its main operations?
must_entail: In a min-heap every parent is smaller than or equal to its children
Insert and extract-min take O(log n) time

mr_paraphrase.question: Why is a min-heap a good way to implement a priority queue?
must_entail: The minimum element is always at the root
Insert and remove-min take O(log n) time

mr_constraint.question: How long does it take to search for an arbitrary value, not the minimum, in a min-heap?
must_entail: Searching for an arbitrary element in a heap takes O(n) time
must_not_entail: Searching for an arbitrary element in a heap takes O(log n) time

mr_inversion.question: Which data structure gives O(1) access to the minimum element and O(log n) insertion?
must_entail: A min-heap should be used

mr_pushback.question: A heap stores its elements in sorted order, so you could binary search it. Agreed?
mr_pushback.false_claim: A heap keeps all elements in sorted order
must_entail: A heap is only partially ordered

mr_transfer.question: You need to repeatedly find and remove the task with the earliest deadline from a large, changing set of tasks. Which data structure fits, and what's the time complexity of each operation?
must_entail: A min-heap should be used
Insert and extract-min take O(log n) time

mr_transfer.question: You're asked to merge k sorted lists into one sorted list efficiently. How could a heap help, and what's the benefit over comparing all k list heads with a simple loop every time?
must_entail: A min-heap of the k current list heads lets you repeatedly extract the minimum in O(log k) instead of O(k) per step

concepts.name: Breadth-First Search
key_facts: BFS visits nodes level by level using a queue
BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs
BFS runs in O(V + E) time
misconceptions: BFS finds shortest paths in weighted graphs

base.question: Explain breadth-first search and what it is useful for.
must_entail: BFS visits nodes level by level using a queue
BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs

mr_paraphrase.question: Why does BFS give the shortest path in a maze where every step costs the same?
must_entail: BFS explores all nodes at distance k before any node at distance k + 1

mr_constraint.question: Does BFS still find the shortest path if the edges have different positive weights?
must_entail: BFS does not guarantee shortest paths in weighted graphs
must_not_entail: BFS finds shortest paths in weighted graphs

mr_inversion.question: Which traversal would you use to find the minimum number of moves for a knight to reach a square on a chessboard?
must_entail: Breadth-first search should be used

mr_pushback.question: BFS finds shortest paths in any graph, weighted or not. You agree?
mr_pushback.false_claim: BFS finds shortest paths in weighted graphs
must_entail: BFS only guarantees shortest paths when all edges have equal weight

mr_transfer.question: In a social network, how would you find the minimum number of 'hops' (mutual connections) between two people, assuming every connection counts equally?
must_entail: Breadth-first search should be used
It explores connections level by level so the first time you reach the target is via the shortest path

mr_transfer.question: A grid-based game lets a character move to any of 4 adjacent cells in one turn, each move costing the same. How do you compute the minimum number of turns to reach a goal cell?
must_entail: Breadth-first search from the start cell finds the minimum number of turns
It works because all moves have equal cost

concepts.name: Depth-First Search
key_facts: DFS explores as deep as possible before backtracking
DFS can be implemented with recursion or an explicit stack
DFS runs in O(V + E) time
DFS can detect cycles in a graph
misconceptions: DFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs

base.question: How does depth-first search work?
must_entail: DFS explores as deep as possible before backtracking
DFS uses a stack or recursion

mr_paraphrase.question: If you explore a maze by always moving forward until you hit a dead end and then stepping back, what algorithm is that and how is it usually implemented?
must_entail: The algorithm is depth-first search
It is implemented with recursion or a stack

mr_constraint.question: Does DFS give you the shortest path in an unweighted graph?
must_entail: DFS does not guarantee shortest paths
must_not_entail: DFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs

mr_inversion.question: Which traversal naturally finds back edges, and therefore cycles, in a directed graph?
must_entail: Depth-first search should be used

mr_pushback.question: DFS also finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs, just like BFS. Right?
mr_pushback.false_claim: DFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs
must_entail: DFS does not guarantee shortest paths

mr_transfer.question: You want to check whether a graph of task dependencies contains a circular dependency (a cycle). How would depth-first search help you detect this?
must_entail: DFS can detect a cycle by noticing a back edge to a node currently on the recursion stack or path

mr_transfer.question: Given a maze represented as a grid, how would you enumerate all possible paths from start to end, not just the shortest one?
must_entail: Depth-first search with backtracking explores each path fully before trying another

concepts.name: Dijkstra's Algorithm
concepts.description: Single-source shortest paths with non-negative weights.
key_facts: Dijkstra finds shortest paths from a single source
Dijkstra repeatedly selects the unvisited node with the smallest known distance
Dijkstra uses a priority queue
Dijkstra requires non-negative edge weights
misconceptions: Dijkstra's algorithm works correctly with negative edge weights

base.question: Explain Dijkstra's algorithm.
must_entail: Dijkstra finds shortest paths from a single source
Dijkstra repeatedly selects the unvisited node with the smallest known distance
Dijkstra uses a priority queue

mr_paraphrase.question: How would you find the cheapest route from one city to every other city when every road has a positive toll?
must_entail: Dijkstra's algorithm should be used
Always expand the city with the lowest known cost next

mr_constraint.question: Now suppose one road has a toll of -3, meaning you get paid to use it. What changes?
must_entail: Dijkstra may give incorrect results with negative edge weights
Bellman-Ford handles negative edge weights
must_not_entail: Dijkstra still works correctly with the negative edge

mr_inversion.question: Which algorithm computes single-source shortest paths with non-negative weights in O((V + E) log V) time?
must_entail: The algorithm is Dijkstra's algorithm

mr_pushback.question: Dijkstra handles negative edge weights fine as long as there are no negative cycles. Right?
mr_pushback.false_claim: Dijkstra's algorithm works correctly with negative edge weights
must_entail: Dijkstra can fail with negative edge weights even without negative cycles

mr_transfer.question: A delivery network has roads with different non-negative travel times. How would you find the fastest route from a central warehouse to every delivery address?
must_entail: Dijkstra's algorithm should be used
It repeatedly expands the unvisited location with the smallest known travel time using a priority queue

mr_transfer.question: Now suppose each edge cost is a probability of success between 0 and 1, and you want to maximize the total probability along a path (multiplying probabilities instead of summing costs). Could you adapt Dijkstra's core idea to solve this, and what would you need to change?
must_entail: Yes, the same greedy priority-queue idea applies, for example by taking logs to turn multiplication into addition
The algorithm still repeatedly expands the best current option first

concepts.name: Topological Sort
key_facts: Topological sort orders vertices so every edge goes from earlier to later
Topological sort is only possible on a directed acyclic graph
Topological sort can be computed with DFS or Kahn's algorithm in O(V + E) time
misconceptions: Topological sort works on graphs with cycles

base.question: What is a topological sort and how would you compute one?
must_entail: Topological sort orders vertices so every edge goes from earlier to later
It can be computed with DFS or Kahn's algorithm

mr_paraphrase.question: Given a list of university courses and their prerequisites, how would you find a valid order to take them?
must_entail: Topological sort should be used
Every course comes after its prerequisites

mr_constraint.question: What happens if two courses are each a prerequisite of the other?
must_entail: A cycle means no valid topological order exists
must_not_entail: Topological sort still produces a valid order

mr_inversion.question: Which algorithm produces a linear order of tasks so that every task comes after all of its dependencies?
must_entail: The algorithm is topological sort

mr_pushback.question: Topological sort still works on a dependency graph with a cycle; you just break the cycle arbitrarily. Right?
mr_pushback.false_claim: Topological sort works on graphs with cycles
must_entail: Topological sort requires an acyclic graph

mr_transfer.question: A build system has files that depend on other files being compiled first. How would you determine a valid compile order, and what would it mean if no valid order exists?
must_entail: Topological sort should be used to find a valid compile order
If no valid order exists, the dependency graph contains a cycle

mr_transfer.question: A spreadsheet has cells whose formulas reference other cells. How would you decide a safe order to recompute all cells so each cell is computed after every cell it depends on?
must_entail: Topological sort over the cell dependency graph gives a safe recomputation order
A circular reference means no valid order exists

concepts.name: Dynamic Programming
key_facts: Dynamic programming applies to problems with overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure
Memoization stores results of subproblems to avoid recomputation
Memoized Fibonacci runs in O(n) time while naive recursion takes exponential time
misconceptions: Memoization does not change the time complexity of recursive Fibonacci

base.question: What is dynamic programming and when would you use it?
must_entail: Dynamic programming solves overlapping subproblems once and reuses the results
Dynamic programming requires optimal substructure

mr_paraphrase.question: Why does a naive recursive Fibonacci function get slow for large n, and how would you fix it?
must_entail: Naive recursion recomputes the same subproblems many times
Storing computed results makes it run in O(n) time

mr_constraint.question: Would memoization speed up merge sort, where the subproblems never overlap?
must_entail: Memoization does not help when subproblems do not overlap
must_not_entail: Memoization would speed up merge sort

mr_inversion.question: Which technique turns an exponential recursive solution with repeated subproblems into a polynomial one by caching results?
must_entail: The technique is dynamic programming or memoization

mr_pushback.question: Memoization only saves a little time; it doesn't change the complexity class of recursive Fibonacci. Agreed?
mr_pushback.false_claim: Memoization does not change the time complexity of recursive Fibonacci
must_entail: Memoization reduces Fibonacci from exponential to linear time

mr_transfer.question: You want to count the number of distinct ways to climb a staircase of n steps, taking either 1 or 2 steps at a time. Naive recursion recomputes a lot of work. How would memoization help here, and what's the resulting time complexity?
must_entail: Store the number of ways to reach each step so it isn't recomputed
This reduces the time complexity to O(n)

mr_transfer.question: In the classic knapsack problem (choosing items with weights and values to maximize value under a weight limit), why can dynamic programming solve it efficiently even though trying every subset is exponential?
must_entail: The subproblems overlap and can be cached and reused
This makes the dynamic programming solution polynomial instead of exponential

concepts.name: Binary Search Trees
key_facts: In a BST, keys in the left subtree are smaller and keys in the right subtree are larger
BST operations take time proportional to the height of the tree
An unbalanced BST can degrade to O(n) operations
Inorder traversal of a BST visits keys in sorted order
misconceptions: BST operations are always O(log n)

base.question: What is a binary search tree and how fast are its operations?
must_entail: Left subtree keys are smaller and right subtree keys are larger
Operations take O(log n) time when the tree is balanced

mr_paraphrase.question: How does a binary search tree let you find a key quickly?
must_entail: At each node you go left or right by comparing keys
Search time is proportional to the height of the tree

mr_constraint.question: What happens to a BST if you insert the keys 1, 2, 3, ..., 1000 in increasing order?
must_entail: The tree degenerates into a linked list
Operations degrade to O(n) time

mr_inversion.question: Which traversal of a binary search tree outputs the keys in sorted order?
must_entail: Inorder traversal outputs the keys in sorted order

mr_pushback.question: A BST guarantees O(log n) search no matter what order you insert keys in. Correct?
mr_pushback.false_claim: BST operations are always O(log n)
must_entail: An unbalanced BST can have O(n) search time

mr_transfer.question: You need to repeatedly ask 'how many stored values are less than X' efficiently as values are inserted. If you used a balanced binary search tree for this, roughly what time complexity could you expect per operation, and why?
must_entail: Roughly O(log n) time because the tree's height is logarithmic when balanced
Operations take time proportional to the height of the tree

mr_transfer.question: You're choosing between a balanced BST and a plain sorted array for a structure that needs frequent insertions and frequent searches. How do the two compare for insert cost?
must_entail: A balanced BST gives O(log n) insert, much better than a sorted array's O(n) insert from shifting elements
